The surprising truth about labour Mobility https://english.radio.cz/why-do-czechs-stay-put-surprising-truth-about-labour-mobility-8893467#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X Czechs are among Europe's least mobile workers. OECD and Eurostat data show they are far less likely than many other Europeans to relocate for work, often preferring to commute instead. Regional geographer and university president Jaroslav Koutský believes geography, family ties and long-standing habits all help explain why. Freedom of movement has been one of the European Union's defining principles ever since Czechia joined the bloc in 2004. The idea was straightforward: workers could move to places where jobs were available, while employers would gain access to a larger pool of labour across the single market. Example? As then European Commissioner for Jobs and Social Rights Nicolas Schmit reminded the European Parliament, labour mobility remains central to the European project: "Labour mobility is a crucial element... It is at the heart of a well-functioning single market," Schmit said, adding that mobility is "a fundamental freedom of the European Union." The reality in Czechia, however, looks rather different. According to OECD and Eurostat data, Czechs are among Europe's least geographically mobile populations. Compared with many neighbouring countries, they are far less likely to move to another region for work. While Austrians, Germans or Swedes relocate much more readily, many Czech workers choose to remain where they live and commute instead. A small country with strong local ties Why that is remains open to debate. Jaroslav Koutský, regional geographer and president of Jan Evangelista Purkyně University in Ústí nad Labem, believes Czechia's geography is part of the explanation. "Maybe we are a small country. Everything is reachable, so we don't need to change the place of living," Koutský says. "We are very fixed on these links and friendships." In other words, relatively short travel distances make commuting easier than moving house, while family and social networks encourage people to stay close to where they grew up. Even university students stay close to home Koutský sees the same tendency among today's university students. Asked whether students still spend weekends in university towns as they once did, he says the opposite has happened. "It's even worse," he says. "They just come for a lecture. And after the lecture they leave. They go home." According to Koutský, even students who rent accommodation often prefer returning to their parents whenever possible rather than building a new social life around the university. That behaviour contrasts with countries such as the United States, Britain or France, where leaving home for university is often seen as an important step towards independence. Whether the Czech pattern is driven primarily by expensive housing, improved transport links or simply a stronger attachment to home remains difficult to quantify. What is clear, however, is that more than twenty years after joining the European Union, many Czechs still make relatively little use of one of its most fundamental freedoms: the freedom to move where the work is. https://www.dw.com/en/at-venice-film-fes.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JLoP Penelope Cruz and Javier Bardem (seen here in a photo from 2017) return to Venice as the stars of Florian Zeller's 'Bunker' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement The Venice Film Festival used to be the place where the awards season put on its best tuxedo. This year, it looks more like a war room, with politics and political cinema set to dominate the red carpet. The 83rd Venice International Film Festival kicks off on September 2 with Danny Boyle's "Ink," a drama about Rupert Murdoch's 1969 takeover of Britain's The Sun tabloid — the origin story of the Murdoch right-wing media empire. Over 11 days on the Lido, audiences will also get films about Israel and Gaza , Russia's war on Ukraine , the CIA-backed coup in Pinochet's Chile, ICE raids in Minneapolis and a tell-all documentary on the world's richest man. Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera has called it Venice's "most political" edition ever. 'Naza,' a documentary by 'No Other Land' directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, runs in the official competition Image: Venice Film Festival/AP Photo/picture alliance Venice goes political This year's competition includes "Naza," a documentary from "No Other Land" Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, examining Israeli military killings of Palestinian civilians in Gaza. US-Russian director Julia Loktev chronicles Russian President Vladimir Putin's crackdown on independent journalism in "My Undesirable Friends Part II — Exile," a sequel to her 2024 doc. DW co-production 'Letters From the Silenced Country' portrays life under repression in Belarus Image: DW/ZDF/Arte Andrei Kutsila's " Letters From the Silenced Country " a DW, ZDF/Arte and TVP co-production about repression in Kutsila's native Belarus, will have its world premiere in Venice. As will Alex Gibney's four-hour Elon Musk documentary "Musk," a film the richest man in the world has already denounced, sight unseen, as a "hit piece." And Laura Poitras, the Oscar-winning director of "Citizenfour," will screen what she describes as a "short horror film," the documentary "They're Here," co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller and built from previously undisclosed footage of ICE's deportation surge in Minneapolis last January . Laura Poitras also won the Golden Lion award in 2022 for best film for 'All the Beauty and the Bloodshed' Image: Domenico Stinellis/AP Photo/picture alliance This is a new look for Venice. Under artistic director Barbera, the festival had until recently cultivated a reputation as a place for movie stars and Oscar campaigns. You go to Venice to watch Timothee Chalamet on the red carpet, or George Clooney and Brad Pitt yucking it up at a press conference. Venice let the other big European festivals — Berlin , and to a lesser degree Cannes — be the homes of political movies and the polemical debates that accompany them. Berlin's political backlash But Berlin's reputation as a festival for activist cinema has taken a major hit. The past three years have seen political debate , primarily over the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, overwhelm discussions of cinema at the Berlinale, to the point where the future of the festival looks in doubt. At this year's Berlinale, jury president Wim Wenders was lambasted online for saying filmmakers " have to stay out of politics ." Later, when Syrian-Palestinian director Abdallah Al-Khatib called out the German government at the awards ceremony for being "partners in the genocide in Gaza by Israel," the backlash nearly cost Berlinale director Tricia Tuttle her job. Venice, by contrast, has spent the past two years leaning into political cinema. How will she react to political questions? Actor Maggie Gyllenhaal is the president of the international jury this year Image: Federico Vespignani/AA/picture alliance Venice leans into controversy Last year saw the world premiere of Kaouther Ben Hania's "The Voice of Hind Rajab." The harrowing docudrama, which recreates the killing, by Israeli forces, of a 5-year-old Palestinian girl and her family in Gaza City, received a 22-minute standing ovation, a Lido record. The Israeli military has recently announced an official investigation into Hind Rajab's death . Just days before, thousands marched on the Lido in protest of the war in Gaza. Filmmakers called on Barbera to label Israel's campaign "a genocide." He didn't go that far, speaking instead of his "huge sadness" over the suffering in Gaza and Palestine. But the Venice boss didn't flinch, then or now, from programming films that address, head-on, the most controversial topics of the day. Danny Boyle's Rupert Murdoch drama 'Ink' opens the festival Image: StudioCanal/AP Photo/picture alliance Ukraine objects to 'DAU' Russian films selected by the festival are also sparking protest. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry, Culture Ministry and its embassy in Italy have issued a formal complaint over Barbera's decision to include Ilya Khrzhanovsky's "DAU," an art house drama about life under Soviet rule in Ukraine, in official competition. Ukraine objects to the film's Russian connections. Khrzhanovsky is Russian-born, though he renounced his Russian citizenship and now lives in exile in Berlin. The film's lead, Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis , still lives and works in Russia and has never publicly condemned Russia's war on Ukraine. Greek-Russian conductor Teodor Currentzis, who stars in 'DAU,' has remained silent on Putin's invasion of Ukraine Image: Getty Images/AFP/S. de Sakutin In a statement, the Ukrainian ministries said programming the film "sends a deeply worrying signal" given the war. Barbera is not backing down. He called the criticism a "smear campaign" from people who haven't seen the film. Khrzhanovsky took to social media on August 20 with his rebuttal: "'DAU' is not an instrument of Russian state cultural policy," he wrote on Facebook. "It is an artistic statement about the nature of totalitarian evil." Stars are still coming Venice hasn't completely abandoned its Hollywood stars. Robert Pattinson, of "Batman" and "Twilight" fame, will hit the Lido this year with "Primetime," playing a controversial US reality TV producer. Robert Pattinson is among the stars expected on the red carpet Image: Luca Carlino/NurPhoto/picture alliance John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell play CIA agents in Chile on the eve of the Pinochet coup in "Wild Horse Nine" from director Martin McDonagh ("Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri"). Real-life couple Javier Bardem and Penelope Cruz star as husband and wife in Florian Zeller's "Bunker," about an architect commissioned to build a nuclear shelter for a billionaire. George Clooney and 93-year-old acting legend Ellen Burstyn will swing by to collect Golden Lion awards for lifetime achievement. George Clooney, a Venice regular, will attend this year to receive an honorary Golden Lion Image: Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Venice also hasn't abandoned its role as a gathering place for cinema's elder statesmen — several of them German. Wim Wenders, fresh off the Berlinale storm, brings an altogether gentler work to the Lido, a 3D documentary on the work of Swiss architect Peter Zumthor. Werner Herzog, the last wild man of '70s German cinema, returns to narrative filmmaking for the first time in seven years in Venice with "Bucking Fastard," starring real-life sisters Kate and Rooney Mara. And for those who want to forget about the world for a moment and just kick back and sing, pop stars Liam and Noel Gallagher are expected on the Lido for the premiere of the Oasis reunion documentary "Don't Look Back in Anger." http://www.cambodiantimes.com/news/27927.text: Aryna Sabalenka opens US Open title defense with win Field Level Media 01 Sep 2026, 04:25 GMT+10 (Photo credit: Robert Deutsch-Imagn Images) Top-seeded Aryna Sabalenka overcame an uneven performance on Monday to begin her bid for a third consecutive U.S. Open title, defeating Colombia's Camila Osorio 6-2, 6-4 in New York. Sabalenka mixed 32 winners with 23 unforced errors but worked through the trouble to win her 14th consecutive match at Flushing Meadows. She also extended her streak of victories in Grand Slam opening rounds to 24. The Belarusian took control of the first set by winning four straight games. Osorio committed five double faults in her first two service games, and Sabalenka eventually pulled away. Osorio made things more difficult in the second set and held two break points, taking a 4-3 lead. Sabalenka saved both, then capitalized on Osorio's ninth double fault to break for 5-4 before serving out the match. 'She played great. She brought the fight, and she battled really well,' Sabalenka said. 'I just tried to stay as aggressive as possible. Sometimes I had to go back just to put the ball in play and move forward as possible.' Sabalenka, who hasn't reached a final since winning Miami in March, will face Russian qualifier Polina Iatcenko in the second round. Two seeded players were knocked out during the early Monday schedule. Taylor Townsend dispatched No. 20 Maja Chwalinska of Poland 6-2, 6-3. Townsend broke serve five times while handing Chwalinska, the French Open runner-up, her fifth loss in six matches since her run in Paris. Spain's Cristina Bucsa eliminated No. 28 Sara Bejlek of the Czech Republic, 7-5, 4-6, 6-1. Bejlek arrived in New York after reaching the Cincinnati semifinals but couldn't carry that momentum into the final set. No. 10 Amanda Anisimova celebrated her 25th birthday by defeating fellow American Ashlyn Krueger 6-1, 6-3. Last year's U.S. Open runner-up struck 25 winners and saved 10 of the 11 break points she faced. 'I'm getting old,' Anisimova said after the match when asked what she's learned since last year's final. 'I don't even look forward to my birthdays anymore.' 'I felt great out there today,' she added. 'I thought I played well so I'm happy about that.' No. 26 Emma Navarro needed two days to secure her place in the second round, completing a 7-6 (6), 6-7 (1), 6-3 victory over France's Lois Boisson. Their match was suspended by rain on Sunday, with Navarro ahead 4-2 in the second set, before Boisson rallied upon the resumption and forced the third. 'I'm just proud of my toughness,' Navarro said. 'It's not easy being that close and losing a tough set.' Another American, Caty McNally, advanced with a 7-5, 6-1 victory over Dutch qualifier Anouk Koevermans. Peyton Stearns wasn't as fortunate, taking the opening set before British qualifier Harriet Dart rallied for a 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 victory. Elsewhere among the seeded players, Czech seventh seed Karolina Muchova cruised past Austria's Sinja Kraus 6-3, 6-0. No. 15 Diana Shnaider of Russia beat Ukraine's Daria Snigur 6-0, 6-4, while No. 21 Anna Kalinskaya defeated fellow Russian Anna Blinkova 6-4, 6-3 and No. 25 Marie Bouzkova of the Czech Republic rolled past France's Elsa Jacquemot 6-2, 6-2. --Field Level Media Watch latest videos Get a daily dose of Cambodian Times news through our daily email, its complimentary and keeps you fully up to date with world and business news as well. Back Credit: Walery Eljasz-Radzikowski/Wikipedia | Domena publiczna Blessed Wincenty Lewoniuk and his 12 Companions were killed for remaining faithful to their Eastern-Catholic faith and their loyalty to the Holy Father. Copy link Archive article Listen to this article share on : Poland could be called a land of martyrs, especially for the remarkable faith many Catholics had during World War II. Yet, even before World War II, Catholics in Poland were being persecuted for their faith and had to endure great suffering in their desire to remain faithful to the Church. This occurred at a time when Poland wasn't even on the maps of Europe and was occupied by a variety of countries, including Russia. During the 19th century, Eastern Catholics in Poland faced pressure to convert to the Russian Orthodox Church, breaking away from the Roman Catholic Church. While some Eastern Catholics submitted to this request, a handful of simple farmers refused to cut ties with the pope. Their refusal eventually cost them their lives. Martyrs of Pratulin Pope Leo praised their heroic example of faithfulness in a recent general audience : Thirty years ago, St. John Paul II beatified Wincenty Lewoniuk and his 12 Companions, martyrs who defended, to the point of shedding their blood, their belonging to the Catholic Church and their unity with the Successor of St. Peter, while remaining faithful to their own Eastern tradition. I entrust to their intercession the cause of unity among Christ’s disciples and Catholics who are persecuted today for their faith. St. John Paul II repeatedly turned to these Polish martyrs during his pontificate, especially whenever he visited Poland. For example, he made a stop in Siedlce in 1999 and highlighted how their example should lead us to contemplate the Church's unity: By their death they confirmed the commitment to Christ of the Catholic Church of Eastern tradition. The same spirit sustained the countless faithful of the Byzantine-Ukrainian Rite, Bishops, priests and lay people, who during 45 years of persecution remained faithful to Christ, preserving their identity as a Church. In this witness, fidelity to Christ is interwoven with fidelity to the Church and becomes a service of unity. Both Pope Leo and St. John Paul II saw these lay martyrs as prime examples for all of us, showing the importance of remaining united to the Barque of Peter. Bl. Wincenty Lewoniuk and his 12 Companions could have easily renounced Rome and embraced the Russian Orthodox faith, but instead, they freely gave their lives up, not willing to sacrifice their union with the Pope. Their example certainly should make us pause and ask ourselves whether we would remain faithful to the Church if we were persecuted in a similar way.
